paras: The Pueblo lynchings of 1882 were the hanging of five men accused of cattle stealing by a masked band in and near Pueblo, Colorado, at the end of March 1882. The band took W. T. Phebus and Jay McGrew from the Pueblo county jail and hanged them from a tree on Santa Fe avenue, then rode about ten miles into the country and hanged two Chastine brothers and Frank Owsby. No one was identified, and the families of the jailed men sued Pueblo county for damages.

Phebus and McGrew were held in the county jail as accused cattle thieves, whom every report called "cattle thieves" or "horse-thieves" outright. According to the Denver Times, Phebus had appeared before Justice Crotty before he was taken to Pueblo, where another prisoner, Sanderson, was held on the same charge.
Dispatches said the lynchers were believed to belong to the county cattle growers' association, formed to protect members' property.

A Pueblo wire dated March 31 said that "a little after 12 o'clock last night" a body of men took the two prisoners from the jail and hanged them near by. Fuller dispatches dated April 1 put the time between 2 and 3 a.m. and the number of men at sixteen. According to one account, the men were masked and gained entry by saying they were deputy sheriffs bringing in a prisoner, then bound and gagged the jailer, whom another paper named as Strait. They hanged Phebus and McGrew to a tree on Santa Fe avenue, within 100 yards of the jail.

The band, said by one report to have grown to twenty-five men, then rode to a ranch about ten miles away, called Chastine's ranch or Reynolds' place on the St. Charles road. There they surrounded the house and seized S. P. (or S. D.) Chastine, his brother, called Billy, Barry or Berry, and Frank Owsby (also spelled Owsley or Orsby). The three were bound, put on horses and hanged in a patch of timber, a grove, or trees near the house, depending on the account.
The hangings were not discovered until late the next morning, and one account said the lynchers were home in bed by daylight.

No arrests, inquest or indictment appear in the coverage. Within a week friends of the lynched men announced a $50,000 suit against the county, arguing that the men had been killed while in the hands of responsible officials. The Denver Times put Mrs. Phebus's claim at $5,000, and by early May papers reported that the families had sued.

The widow went to Pueblo for her husband's body and vowed to bring "the murderers" to justice. She rejected the cattle growers theory, telling the Denver Times that the Foremans, Sanderson's brothers-in-law, had arranged the lynching, and asking why the lynchers had not also taken Sanderson.

The story spread mainly as a short wire item headed "Cattle Thieves Lynched" or "Speedy Justice" that called the victims cattle thieves. Some versions carried a Denver dateline, so Eastern papers placed the lynching in Denver; others said "South Pueblo" or "Pueblo, N. M."

Weekly summaries called it a "wholesale lynching affair" and said one of "the gang" was left, "and a necktie is ready for him." The Delaware Daily Republican headlined its account "Sixteen Masked Cattle Dealers Hang Five Men to Trees in One Night."

The Cheyenne Daily Leader called the five "well-known cattle thieves" in the same column that warned that "Lynch law is becoming epidemic in the west." The Denver Times, quoted in Cheyenne, wrote that if taxpayers had to pay for "every such exhibition of mob violence it may become customary to protect prisoners from being murdered." In May the Barbour County Index of Kansas, whose county McGrew had once lived in, called the killing murder "without a shadow of justification" and said those who knew him would need positive proof of his guilt. No paper gave the race of any of the five men.

Early reports put the jail lynching on Thursday night, March 30, while dispatches datelined April 1 said "this morning." The wires attributed the lynching to cattle growers' association members, while Mrs. Phebus blamed Sanderson's relatives, and the Kansas editor disputed McGrew's guilt.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A masked band took two accused cattle thieves from the Pueblo county jail and hanged them, then hanged three more men at a ranch (A4, A5, A7).
Sixteen or more men with no lawful authority took two prisoners from jail and hanged them and three other men as cattle thieves (A4, A5, A7); the race of the victims is never stated.

The Associated Press wire (A1, A4, A7) and a separate Denver Tribune Pueblo special (A5) agree on the jail hangings and the three further hangings; only the identity of the lynchers and the men's guilt are disputed (A12, A27).

framing.detail: Headlines 'Speedy Justice' and 'Cattle Thieves Lynched' named the victims as thieves and repeated the association theory.
Weekly summaries called it a 'wholesale lynching affair' and joked that 'a necktie is ready' for the last of the gang.
The Cheyenne Daily Leader called the five 'well-known cattle thieves' while warning that lynch law was 'becoming epidemic in the west'.
The Denver Times called it 'mob violence' and hoped damage suits would make officials protect prisoners from being 'murdered'.
The Barbour County Index called McGrew's killing murder 'without a shadow of justification'.
